endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Note that not all organizations will be using data to develop or train models, but must still have data preparation SOPs for data that will be input into the model for use, used to fine-tune the model, or shared with third-party vendors.

endorsements.title: Building a Safe and Transparent Workflow for Large Language Model (LLM)-Assisted Clinical Trials and Prediction Models: A Technical Report
endorsements.quote: Maintain full search strings, databases, dates/limits, de-duplication criteria, and a PRISMA flow with screening logs (see Table 3 ) [ 11 ].

endorsements.title: An auditable and source-verified framework for clinical AI decision support: integrating retrieval-augmented generation with data provenance
endorsements.quote: Provenance and evidence grading: Every content item is tagged with comprehensive provenance metadata, including authors, publication dates, and source types.

endorsements.title: From reviews to real-time: dynamic evidence in dentistry
endorsements.quote: Clear standards for corpus curation, retrieval quality, transparency of outputs, and integration with systematic review processes are essential.

endorsements.title: A conceptual agentic AI architecture for MASLD-associated significant fibrosis in primary care
endorsements.quote: Any retrieval-augmented approach should implement source whitelisting, change logs, and a governance gate before surfaced content influences recommendations (Fig 1).

evidence.title: Reducing Hallucinations and Trade-Offs in Responses in Generative AI Chatbots for Cancer Information: Development and Evaluation Study
evidence.outcome: Effect of vetted versus unvetted retrieval corpus on hallucination rate
evidence.effect: Google-retrieval chatbots had 18% hallucinations among answered questions vs 2% for CIS chatbots; Google OR 9.4 (95% CI 1.2-17.5, P<.01) versus CIS.
evidence.quote: In multivariate analysis, adjusting for other factors, models with RAG reference data from Google search results were more likely to generate hallucinations compared with those with RAG reference data from CIS, with an OR of 9.4 (95% CI 1.2‐17.5; P <.01).

evidence.title: A Self-Controlled Benchmark of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models on Clinical Guideline Questions
evidence.outcome: Retrieval recall and citation groundedness of a documented guideline RAG corpus
evidence.effect: Retrieval recall@5 was 92%; citation groundedness rose from 0% to 51-89% deterministically from retrieval logs.
evidence.quote: Deterministically from the retrieval logs, citation groundedness rose from 0% to 51-89% and retrieval recall@5 was 92%.
evidence.sample_unit: evaluations (50 questions x 6 models x 3 repetitions)

evidence.title: Real-world deployment and evaluation of PEri-operative AI CHatbot (PEACH): a large language model chatbot for peri-operative medicine
evidence.outcome: Hallucinations and deviations when LLM is grounded in embedded institutional protocols
evidence.quote: Hallucinations and deviations were minimal (1/240 and 2/240, respectively).

evidence.title: Rethinking Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medicine: A Large-Scale, Systematic Expert Evaluation and Practical Insights
evidence.effect: Only 22% of top-16 passages were relevant.
evidence.quote: Contrary to expectation, standard RAG often degraded performance: only 22% of top-16 passages were relevant, evidence selection remained weak (precision 41-43%, recall 27-49%), and factuality and completeness dropped by up to 6% and 5%, respectively, compared with non-RAG variants.
evidence.sample_unit: model outputs annotated by 18 medical experts (80,502 annotations; 200 queries)

evidence.title: Comparative Evaluation of Advanced Chunking for Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Large Language Models for Clinical Decision Support
evidence.effect: Basic fixed-size chunking had precision 0.17, recall 0.40, and F1 0.24.
evidence.quote: Conversely, the basic fixed-size chunking model performed lowest, with 0.17 (0.04–0.32) precision, 0.40 (0.10–0.70) recall, and an F1 of 0.24 (0.00–0.39), indicating that fewer than one in five retrieved passages were relevant and less than half of the relevant evidence was found.

evidence.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medical Decision-Making in Emergency Care
evidence.venue: Annual International Conference of the IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society. IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society. Annual International Conference
evidence.effect: Performance deficit and error susceptibility were predominantly attributed to constraints in automated chunk splitting.
evidence.quote: This performance deficit and error susceptibility of the RAG system was predominantly attributable to the constraints inherent in the automated splitting of chunks.

evidence.title: MAM-AI: An On-Device Medical Retrieval-Augmented Generation System for Nurses and Midwives in Zanzibar
evidence.outcome: answer quality when corpus lacks passage
evidence.effect: Answers were specific/actionable when corpus held the right passage, vague when it did not.
evidence.quote: Corpus quality is decisive for the same reason: where the corpus holds the right passage the answer is specific and actionable, and where it does not it goes vague.

evidence.title: Cosine Similarity Conflates Clinically Distinct Cancer Variants: A Case for Typed-Graph Retrieval in Precision Oncology Decision Support
evidence.outcome: Wrong paired variant retrieved in top 5 in corpus-level ranked retrieval
evidence.effect: Wrong paired variant appeared in top 5 for 75% to 100% of queries under biomedical encoders over a 52-document corpus.
evidence.quote: In corpus-level ranked retrieval over a 52-document corpus, the wrong paired variant appeared in the top 5 for 75% to 100% of queries under the biomedical encoders.

evidence.title: Measurement of retrieved chunk quality from real-world knowledge in retrieval-augmented generation: A Phase 1 foundational study
evidence.effect: Median scores were 2.0 or below across all five metrics; fewer than 20% reached score ≥4.
evidence.quote: The results revealed substantial quality limitations in the A-line chunks: the median scores were 2.0 or below across all five metrics, with fewer than 20% of the chunks reaching practical utility thresholds (score of 4 or higher).
evidence.sample_unit: retrieved chunks (594 baseline A-line, 6 optimized B-line)

evidence.title: Improving accuracy of GPT-3/4 results on biomedical data using a retrieval-augmented language model
evidence.effect: For question #13, retrieval returned multiple myeloma and chronic lymphocytic leukemia articles rather than DLBCL material, and the summarizer produced an incorrect answer.
evidence.quote: For example, question #13 asked about minimal residual disease (MRD) in DLBCL, but the document retriever returned articles about MRD in multiple myeloma and chronic lymphocytic leukemia—two distinct hematological malignancies from DLBCL.

evidence.title: Development and performance of a generative pretrained transformer for diabetes care
evidence.outcome: Accuracy and citation inclusion of curated-source diabetes GPT responses
evidence.effect: Overall accuracy 91.7%, citations included in 93.3% of responses, rationale in 100%; accuracy lower for insulin-related items (82.3%).
evidence.quote: Diabetes Help GPT showed high overall accuracy (91.7 %), with 100 % rationale inclusion, 93.3 % citations, 84.8 % disclaimers, and minimal emoji use (13.3 %).

commentary.bottom_line: Two offline studies suggest that vetted, documented retrieval corpora may reduce hallucinations and make citations traceable, but neither tests the act of defining and registering corpus criteria in live care. Hazard studies show that poor sources and indexing degrade retrieval, which supports the concern without showing that a registry solves it.

perspectives.view: Two studies test the practice, and both are offline or benchmark evaluations with surrogate outcomes. In one, Google-retrieval chatbots hallucinated in 18% of answered questions versus 2% for CIS chatbots using a vetted corpus (OR 9.4, 95% CI 1.2-17.5). Neither study tests registration itself, so certainty is very low for indirectness and imprecision.

Hazard studies show retrieval failures that can reach answers. Only 22% of top-16 passages were relevant in one study, and off-target articles retrieved for a DLBCL question led to an incorrect answer in another. A documented guideline corpus raised citation groundedness from 0% to 51-89%, which suggests documentation may make errors traceable. No study measured patient harm.

Indexing choices appear to affect retrieval quality. Fixed-size chunking yielded precision 0.17 and recall 0.40, and a German study of 100 cases attributed most errors to automated chunk splitting. One real deployment grounded in embedded institutional protocols recorded 1 hallucination in 240 queries. No study measured the staff time needed to document and maintain a corpus registry.

Studies conducted in Japan and Germany, including one test of the practice, were classified as covering limited English or non-English populations. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy patients, and none examined whether registered corpora contain materials suited to those groups.

The CHAI playbook states that organizations must keep data preparation procedures for data input into models, even when they do not train models. The other three endorsements are commentaries. No study examined whether a corpus registry satisfies FDA, ONC, or state requirements, so the policy case rests on framework guidance rather than tested outcomes.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares deployments with and without documented, registered corpus inclusion criteria, sources, and indexing methods. Prospective evaluations in live clinical workflows should measure hallucination rates, citation traceability, audit time, and maintenance burden, and they should include safety-net and limited English proficiency settings.
commentary.underserved_note: One testing study, conducted in Japan, was classified as including a limited English or non-English population, but no test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy patients. That classification does not establish relevance to limited English proficiency patients in U.S. care, so the benefit for those groups remains untested.
